title: Python Fundamentals for AI
summary: Python is the language of AI. Its readable syntax and vast library ecosystem make it the default for machine learning. Today you learn the core building blocks: storing data in variables, controlling flow with conditionals and loops, and packaging lo
content:
# Python Fundamentals for AI ##### Why the whole field speaks one language In 2007, if you wanted to do serious numerical work you probably used MATLAB, R, or C++. Python was considered a scripting language — pleasant, but slow and not really for mathematics. Then NumPy gave Python fast arrays backed by C. Pandas gave it dataframes. scikit-learn gave it machine learning with a consistent interface. PyTorch and TensorFlow gave it deep learning. Each library made the next one more valuable, and within a decade Python had won by network effect. The practical consequence for you: **essentially every AI tool, tutorial, paper implementation and job posting assumes Python.** Learning it well is not one option among several — it is the entry requirement. The good news is that Python was designed for readability. Compare printing the numbers 1 to 5 in Java and Python: ```java // Java public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { System.out.println(i); } } } ``` ```python # Python for i in range(1, 6): print(i) ``` Less ceremony, more meaning. That difference compounds enormously when the code is a machine learning pipeline rather than a loop. ##### Variables and data types A **variable** is a name bound to a value. Python figures out the type — you never declare it. ```python model_name = "resnet50" # str — text epochs = 30 # int — whole number learning_rate = 0.001 # float — decimal is_training = True # bool — True or False best_checkpoint = None # NoneType — deliberately no value print(type(learning_rate)) # ``` Note `True`, `False` and `None` are capitalized — a frequent typo when moving between languages. **Strings** are text, and you will manipulate them constantly when cleaning data: ```python raw = " Iris-Setosa " print(raw.strip()) # "Iris-Setosa" — remove outer whitespace print(raw.strip().lower()) # "iris-setosa" print(raw.strip().replace("-", "_")) # "Iris_Setosa" print(raw.strip().split("-")) # ['Iris', 'Setosa'] print(len(raw.strip())) # 11 ``` **f-strings** build readable output, and you will use them in every training loop you ever write: ```python epoch, loss, acc = 12, 0.0342, 0.9614 print(f"Epoch {epoch:>3} | loss {loss:.4f} | acc {acc:.2%}") # Epoch 12 | loss 0.0342 | acc 96.14% ``` The format specifiers are worth learning: `:.4f` gives four decimal places, `:.2%` renders a fraction as a percentage, `:>3` right-aligns in three characters. Neat training logs are a small thing that makes debugging much easier. **Numbers** behave as expected, with three operators worth knowing: ```python print(7 / 2) # 3.5 — true division, always returns a float print(7 // 2) # 3 — floor division print(7 % 2) # 1 — remainder (used constantly for "every nth item") print(2 ** 10) # 1024 — exponentiation ``` ##### Operators and expressions Comparison operators return booleans: `==` (equal), `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`. Logical operators are words rather than symbols: `and`, `or`, `not`. ```python accuracy = 0.94 epochs_done = 30 if accuracy > 0.90 and epochs_done >= 25: print("Ready to evaluate on the test set") ``` Two Python-specific behaviours worth internalizing early. **Chained comparisons** read naturally and are genuinely useful for range checks: ```python if 0.0 <= learning_rate <= 1.0: print("learning rate in valid range") ``` **Truthiness.** Empty things are false. `if not data:` is `True` when `data` is `[]`, `{}`, `""`, `0` or `None` — a compact way to check "is this missing or empty," which you will use when validating inputs. And the classic confusion: `=` assigns, `==` compares. Writing `if x = 5:` is a syntax error, which is Python protecting you. ##### Conditionals ```python loss = 0.42 if loss < 0.1: status = "excellent" elif loss < 0.5: status = "acceptable" elif loss < 1.0: status = "needs work" else: status = "something is wrong" print(f"Loss {loss} → {status}") ``` **Indentation is the syntax.** Python has no braces; the indented block *is* the body of the `if`. Use four spaces, consistently, and never mix tabs with spaces — `IndentationError` and `TabError` are the most common early frustrations, and both come from that. A compact form you will meet in real code: ```python device = "cuda" if gpu_available else "cpu" # ternary expression ``` ##### Loops The `for` loop iterates over a sequence — this is how you process datasets: ```python losses = [0.92, 0.61, 0.44, 0.38, 0.35] for epoch, loss in enumerate(losses, start=1): print(f"Epoch {epoch}: loss = {loss:.3f}") # range() generates numbers for i in range(0, 10, 2): # start, stop (exclusive), step print(i) # 0 2 4 6 8 ``` `enumerate()` gives you the index alongside the value, which saves the clumsy manual counter beginners often write. Its companion is `zip()`, which walks two sequences together: ```python predictions = [1, 0, 1, 1, 0] actuals = [1, 0, 0, 1, 0] correct = 0 for pred, actual in zip(predictions, actuals): if pred == actual: correct += 1 print(f"Accuracy: {correct / len(actuals):.1%}") # Accuracy: 80.0% ``` The `while` loop runs until a condition becomes false — used for training until convergence: ```python loss, epoch = 1.0, 0 while loss > 0.05 and epoch < 100: # ALWAYS bound it, or it may never stop loss *= 0.85 epoch += 1 print(f"Converged after {epoch} epochs (loss {loss:.4f})") ``` Inside any loop, `continue` skips to the next iteration and `break` exits entirely: ```python for value in [3, -1, 7, None, 12]: if value is None or value < 0: continue # skip invalid data print(value ** 2) ``` That pattern — skip the bad records, process the rest — appears in essentially every data-cleaning script you will write. ##### Functions and scope A **function** packages logic under a name so you can reuse it. ```python def normalize(values: list[float]) -> list[float]: """Scale values to the 0-1 range (min-max normalization).""" lo, hi = min(values), max(values) if hi == lo: # guard against divide-by-zero return [0.0] * len(values) return [(v - lo) / (hi - lo) for v in values] def accuracy(predictions: list[int], actuals: list[int]) -> float: """Fraction of predictions that match the actual labels.""" if len(predictions) != len(actuals): raise ValueError("predictions and actuals must be the same length") matches = sum(1 for p, a in zip(predictions, actuals) if p == a) return matches / len(actuals) print(normalize([10, 20, 30, 40])) # [0.0, 0.333..., 0.666..., 1.0] print(accuracy([1, 0, 1], [1, 1, 1])) # 0.666... ``` Several habits are worth adopting from the start. **Type hints** (`list[float]`, `-> float`) document intent and let editors catch mistakes. **Docstrings** say what the function does in one line. **Guard clauses** handle the bad case first and return early. And each function does **one thing** with a verb-like name. **Default and keyword arguments** make functions flexible: ```python def train(data, epochs=10, learning_rate=0.01, verbose=True): ... train(my_data) # uses all defaults train(my_data, epochs=50, learning_rate=0.001) # keyword args, order-independent ``` One trap that catches everyone once: **never use a mutable default**. `def add_item(item, bucket=[])` creates *one* list shared across every call. Use `bucket=None` and create the list inside. **Scope** determines what a function can see: it can read variables defined outside it, but assigning to a name creates a new local variable rather than changing the outer one. Prefer passing values in as parameters and returning results out — code that depends on hidden global state is hard to test and hard to reason about. ##### Modules and imports A **module** is a `.py` file. Import it to reuse its contents: ```python import math # whole module from statistics import mean, stdev # specific names import numpy as np # with an alias — the universal convention print(math.sqrt(16)) # 4.0 print(mean([1, 2, 3, 4])) # 2.5 ``` The aliases `np` for NumPy, `pd` for Pandas and `plt` for Matplotlib are conventions so universal that using anything else will confuse every reader of your code, including your future self. Your own files work the same way. With `utils.py` containing your `normalize` function: ```python from utils import normalize, accuracy ``` ##### Virtual environments and pip This is the piece beginners skip and later regret. Different projects need different library versions. Project A needs TensorFlow 2.10; project B needs 2.16. Installing globally means they conflict, and you eventually break an environment badly enough to reinstall Python. A **virtual environment** is an isolated set of packages per project: ```bash # Create it (once per project) python3 -m venv .venv # Activate it (every session) source .venv/bin/activate # macOS / Linux .venv\Scripts\activate # Windows # Your prompt now shows (.venv) pip install numpy pandas scikit-learn matplotlib jupyter # Record exactly what is installed pip freeze > requirements.txt # Someone else — or future you — recreates it pip install -r requirements.txt deactivate # when you're done ``` Add `.venv/` to `.gitignore`; commit `requirements.txt`. That pair is what makes a project reproducible on another machine. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Install Python 3.11+] --> B[Create project folder] B --> C[python3 -m venv .venv] C --> D[Activate the environment] D --> E[pip install libraries] E --> F[Write code] F --> G[pip freeze > requirements.txt] G --> H[git init + .gitignore
excluding .venv/] ``` ##### Common mistakes - **Mixing tabs and spaces** — use four spaces everywhere. - **`=` instead of `==`** in a condition. - **Mutable default arguments** (`def f(x=[])`). - **Off-by-one with `range()`** — `range(5)` is 0–4, not 1–5. - **Modifying a list while looping over it** — build a new list instead. - **Installing packages globally** instead of in a virtual environment. - **Forgetting to activate the environment**, then wondering why an import fails. - **`"3" + 4`** — a `TypeError`; convert with `int()` or `float()` first. - **Naming a file `random.py` or `math.py`**, which shadows the standard library and produces baffling errors. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **set up Python and a virtual environment**, then write a script that classifies numbers as prime using a **function and a loop**. The primality check is a good first exercise because it exercises loops, conditionals, the modulo operator and early returns all at once — and because the naive version is easy to write and then obviously improvable (checking divisors only up to the square root). The mini project is a **command-line grade calculator** that takes scores, computes averages and letter grades, and **handles invalid input**. That last requirement is the interesting one: what happens when someone types "ninety" or leaves the field blank? Handling it gracefully rather than crashing is the difference between a script and a program. For the assignment, write **five small programs** — temperature converter, FizzBuzz, factorial, palindrome check, simple calculator — and **push them to GitHub**. Do not skip the pushing. Getting Git working now, while the code is trivial, means it is not a second obstacle later when you have a project worth publishing. Tomorrow's material assumes you can create and run Python files comfortably; these five will get you there. ##### Key takeaways - Python won the AI ecosystem through compounding libraries, so fluency in it is the entry requirement rather than a preference. - Indentation defines blocks — use four spaces consistently, and remember `True`/`False`/`None` are capitalized. - `for` with `enumerate()` and `zip()`, plus `continue` and `break`, covers most data-processing loops you will write. - Write small functions with type hints, docstrings and guard clauses; avoid mutable default arguments and hidden global state. - Create a virtual environment per project, install with pip, commit `requirements.txt` and gitignore `.venv/` — reproducibility starts here.
